title: Protest of Maryland Office of People's Counsel re PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s compliance filing submitted on 02/23/2026 under ER26-1479.

documents.name: OPC Protest ER26-1479.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                         BEFORE THE
            FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C.        DOCKET NO. ER26-1479-000



PROTEST OF THE MARYLAND OFFICE OF PEOPLE’S COUNSEL ON PJM
                   COMPLIANCE FILING

                              DAVID S. LAPP
                              PEOPLE’S COUNSEL

                              William F. Fields
                              Deputy People’s Counsel

                              Philip L. Sussler
                              Senior Assistant People’s Counsel

                              Mark S. Byrd
March 16, 2026                Assistant People’s Counsel
           Pursuant to Rules 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s Rules of

Practice and Procedure,1 the Maryland Office of People’s Counsel (“MdOPC”)

respectfully submits the following protest regarding PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s

(“PJM”) compliance filing submitted on February 23, 2026 in the above captioned

proceeding (hereinafter, “February 23 Compliance Filing”) that proposes tariff revisions

with respect to behind-the-meter generation, and services available for co-located load,

among other proposed revisions, to implement the Commission’s December 18, 2025

compliance directives in the co-located load show-cause proceeding (“Show Cause

Order”).2



                                        INTRODUCTION

          PJM’s February 23 Compliance Filing proposes tariff revisions in compliance with

the Commission’s Show Cause Order, that attempt to create clarity and consistency with

regard to the rates, terms, and conditions applicable to co-location arrangements.

Particularly, the February 23 Compliance Filing proposes to clarify how both new and

existing generation can interconnect co-location arrangements.

          However, PJM’s proposed revisions are incompatible with the Statement of

Principles agreed by the White House-Governors, dated January 15, 2026 (hereinafter,




1
    18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211 (2025).
2
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“Show Cause Order”).


                                                   1
 the “Statement of Principles”)3, the Ratepayer Protection Pledge4 issued by the White

House dated March 4, 2026, and PJM’s recent initiative toward implementing a reliability

backstop auction (“RBA”) that began after the Show Cause Order (and in response to the

Statement of Principles), and which is intended to attract revenue specifically toward new

generation—not existing generators.

        The proposed revisions contained in PJM’s February 23 Compliance Filing

directly contradict PJM’s plan for the RBA. Whereas PJM’s proposed revisions facilitate

co-location arrangements for both new and existing generators, PJM’s RBA will procure

only new generation for co-located loads, not existing generation. In other words, the

Statement of Principles (and the RBA intended to implement one of its pillars)

contemplates new generation to offset the adverse impact of data centers on supply-

demand. But it is unclear how PJM will achieve this RBA benefit if existing generators

can serve co-located load without limit. Additionally, PJM’s proposal does not clarify

how residential and other ratepayers will be protected, as required by the Ratepayer

Protection Pledge, from the costs of acquiring new generation to replace existing




3
  With respect to a future RBA, the Statement of Principles provides in relevant part: “Provide Revenue
Certainty to New Generation: Provide 15-year price certainty for new capacity resources. This can be
accomplished by holding a Reliability Backstop Auction to procure new capacity resources commencing
no later than September 2026” (emphasis in original). Regarding protecting residential customers, the
Statement of Principles states that due to data centers’ size and risks they pose to resource adequacy,
“PJM should allocate the cost of any new capacity procured through the aforementioned Reliability
Backstop Auction to load serving entities (LSEs) with new data centers that have not self-procured new
capacity or agreed to be curtailable. Any remaining costs should be allocated to LSEs based on their
remaining net short positions”) (emphasis in original).
4
  The Ratepayer Protection Pledge provides that the pledging companies agree to, in relevant part: “build,
bring or buy the new generation resources needed to satisfy their new energy demands, paying the full
cost of those resources whether by building or buying from, new or otherwise additive power plants.”


                                                    2
 generation that has chosen to shift to a co-location arrangement under the proposed tariff

revisions.

          Thus, rather than providing clarity and consistency as the Commission intended,

intervening events have resulted in the proposed tariff contradicting PJM’s ongoing

initiatives. As a result, the proposed tariff revisions are unjust and unreasonable in their

present form, without addressing and avoiding their incompatibility with the Statement of

Principles and Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and understanding how the proposed tariff

revisions will interact with the RBA. At a minimum, the Commission should defer action

on the proposed co-location framework until PJM’s RBA proposal is finalized.



                                          BACKGROUND

Show Cause Proceeding

          On February 20, 2025, the Commission initiated a show cause proceeding under

section 206 of the Federal Power Act to determine whether PJM’s tariff is just and

reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential without provisions addressing

with sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply

to Co-Location Arrangements.5 On December 18, 2025, the Commission determined that

PJM’s tariff is unjust and unreasonable, explaining that the tariff:

          does not contain provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency
          the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to Interconnection
          Customers serving Co-Located Load, including generators serving Co-
          Located Load in a configuration with special protection schemes to prevent
          the Co-Located Load from taking energy from the transmission system.6
5
    See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025).
6
    Show Cause Order at P 249.


                                                    3
 The Commission found that:

        the absence of such provisions leaves entities unable to determine what
        steps they must take to effectuate Co-Location Arrangements, which creates
        uncertainty that has resulted in disparate treatment in PJM, where
        transmission owners have taken different approaches to performing the
        necessary steps that apply to Interconnection Customers seeking to serve
        Co-Located Load through a Co-Location Arrangement, leading to no
        consistent understanding of entities’ responsibilities with respect to their
        planned Co-Location Arrangements. We also find that PJM’s Tariff is unjust
        and unreasonable because it does not include transmission services that
        reflect an Eligible Customer taking service on behalf of a Co-Located Load
        that is willing and able to limit its energy withdrawals from the
        transmission system under certain conditions. Further, we find that PJM’s
        Tariff is unjust and unreasonable because it does not address charges related
        to Co-Located Loads’ use of regulation and black start services, which
        introduces the risk that Co-Located Loads may benefit from regulation and
        black start services without contributing to cost recovery for such services
        and, thereby, the risk that costs may be allocated entirely to other
        transmission customers and passed through to residential customers, among
        others.7

        The Commission clarified that an existing generating facility may not begin

serving Co-Located Load that is not Network Load until it has delisted its Capacity

Interconnection Rights for the portion of the generating facility to be designated to serve

any Co-Located Load that is not receiving NITS.8

        The Commission directed PJM to revise its tariff to provide sufficient clarity

regarding the responsibilities of existing interconnection customers seeking to serve co-

located load using their generating facilities.9 The Commission also directed PJM to file

tariff changes specifying that an interconnection customer seeking to serve co-located


7
  Id. P 175.
8
  Id. P 230.
9
  Id. P 225.


                                              4
 load using an existing generating facility must bear the costs of all network upgrades that

PJM finds are necessary to preserve transmission system reliability for existing

transmission customers.10

        Furthermore, the Show Cause Order also required that PJM define “Co-Located

Load” as a “configuration [that] refers to end-use customer load that is physically

connected to the facilities of an existing or planned Customer Facility on the

Interconnection Customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection to the PJM Transmission

System.”11

February 23 Compliance Filing

        PJM’s February 23 Compliance Filing generally sets forth the relative obligations

of project developers seeking to serve co-located load, and PJM. The proposal defines

“Co-Located Generating Facility” as “an existing or planned Generating Facility that is

physically connected to a Co-Located Load,” and “Co-Located Load” as “a configuration

that refers to end-use customer load that is physically connected to the facilities of an

existing or planned Generating Facility on the Project Developer’s side of the Point of

Change in Ownership to the Transmission Provider’s Transmission System.”12

Importantly, these definitions appear to accommodate not only new generators, but

existing generators seeking to serve co-located load.

11

12

                                                    5
         Additionally, the February 23 Compliance Filing proposes tariff revisions

requiring that “[a] Project Developer whose planned modifications include Co-Located

Load configuration shall be required to enter into a Necessary Studies Agreement with

Transmission Provider in the form set forth in Tariff, Part IX, Subpart G.”13 The proposed

tariff revisions would require a Project Developer to provide the Transmission Provider

with “the amount of reduction to Capacity Interconnection Rights to facilitate the Co-

Located Load configuration.”14 The proposed revisions also provide that:

        Project Developer shall be responsible for the costs of any modifications or
        Network Upgrades identified by Transmission Provider, as applicable, as a
        result of the change to the Interconnection Service Agreement or
        Generation Interconnection Agreement to serve Co-Located Load,
        including to reflect any reduction in Capacity Interconnection Rights.15

“Capacity Interconnection Rights” (“CIRs”) are previously defined in PJM’s tariff as “the

rights to input generation as a Generation Capacity Resource into the Transmission

System at the Point of Interconnection where the generating facilities connect to the

Transmission System.”16 Thus, the proposed revisions appear to accommodate new

generators seeking to serve co-located load, as well as existing generators seeking to

serve co-located load by reducing their CIRs, and thus their ability to input generation

onto PJM’s transmission system.

 White House and PJM Governors Statement of Principles and White House Pledge

       On January 15, 2026, the National Energy Dominance Council within the White

House and thirteen governors of states within PJM signed the Statement of Principles

urging PJM to expeditiously file proposed tariff revisions with the Commission that

reflect a set of principles for how generation capacity for data centers should be procured,

and how costs should be allocated to data centers to protect residential customers.17

Specifically, under these principles, PJM should hold a RBA to procure new capacity

resources, with the costs of such new capacity going primarily to load serving entities

with new data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed to be

curtailable.18

       On March 4, 2026, the White House issued the Ratepayer Protection Pledge that

companies will build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity needed

to satisfy their new energy demands, paying the full cost of those resources whether by

building, or buying from, new or otherwise additive power plants.19 The pledge also

provides that where possible, these companies will also add more capacity that serves the

broader public by increasing supply.20

                                         PROTEST

I.      PJM’s proposed tariff revisions are unjust and unreasonable because it is
        unclear how they will interact with PJM’s implementation of the RBA.

        As explained by the Commission in the Show Cause Order, PJM’s tariff is unjust

and unreasonable because it does not contain provisions addressing with sufficient clarity

or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to generators serving

Co-Located Load and Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Co-

Located Load.21 However, in light of the Statement of Principles issued jointly by the

White House and thirteen governors of states within PJM, the Ratepayer Protection

Pledge, and PJM’s subsequent responsive work toward instituting a RBA to be held

toward the end of 2026, PJM’s tariff remains without sufficient clarity and consistency.

        The Statement of Principles directed PJM to hold an RBA to procure new capacity

resources.22 The Statement of Principles further urges that costs of such new capacity

should go primarily to load serving entities with new data centers that have not self-

procured new capacity or agreed to be curtailable.23 The Ratepayer Protection Pledge also

commits the major data center developers to procure new capacity resources to serve

their needs. Thus, the thrust of the Statement of Principles and the Ratepayer Protection

Pledge is that generally new data centers should pay for new capacity.

        Under this framework, new data centers that are not served by self-procured new

co-located generation could be subject to higher costs from the load serving entity as



21
   See Show Cause Order at P 2.
22
   See Statement of Principles at 1.
23
   See id.


                                             8
 result of the RBA. But PJM’s proposed tariff revisions do not explain how existing

capacity resources that shift to co-located arrangements with new data centers would be

treated relative to the RBA. For example, it is unclear whether the capacity of existing

generators that enter co-location arrangements with new data center load would be added

to the capacity required to be procured in the RBA, or to the capacity procured in the

regular base residual auction (“BRA”).

       If the capacity of existing generation that shifts to serve new co-located data center

load is added to the BRA, ratepayers would be saddled with enormous costs that should

be assigned to the co-located load, in contravention of the Statement of Principles and the

Ratepayer Protection Pledge. For example, recent analysis by PJM’s Independent Market

Monitor concluded that if 1,000 UCAP MW of nuclear capacity in Maryland was

removed—due to shifting to serving a co-located load for example—total market

revenues for the 2025/2026 BRA would increase by more than $3.6 billion.24 Yet PJM’s

compliance filing provides no explanation as to how such costs would be paid by new co-

located data center load rather than being shifted to existing ratepayers.

       PJM’s compliance filing thus leaves significant and fundamental questions

unanswered with respect to how existing generation can serve new co-located data center

load. Without providing more details regarding how the proposal will align with PJM’s

plans for the RBA, PJM’s proposal remains unclear and inconsistent with the Statement




24
  See Comments to the Maryland PSC Senate Bill 1 Co-location Study Administrative Docket PC 61
(Sep. 24, 2024) at 3,
https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/filings/2024/IMM_Comments_MDPSC_PC61_20240924.pdf.


                                                9
 of Principles underpinning the RBA. This lack of clarity and consistency causes PJM’s

tariff to remain unjust and unreasonable. At a minimum, the Commission should defer

action on the proposed revisions until PJM announces details regarding its planned RBA,

including specifics on how the RBA will interact with co-located arrangements to ensure

that new co-located loads pay the costs of any new capacity.



                                     CONCLUSION

       The issuance of the Statement of Principles by the White House and thirteen

governors of states within PJM calling for an RBA to serve new data center load and the

Ratepayer Protection Pledge are salient intervening events that have occurred since the

Show Cause Order issued. However, despite the significance of PJM’s work toward

implementing an RBA, fundamental issues surrounding how existing generators that shift

to serve co-located load under PJM’s proposed tariff revisions will be treated relative to

the RBA remain unaddressed. As a result, PJM’s proposed revisions do not provide the

clarity and consistency required by the Show Cause Order. PJM’s proposed tariff

revisions thus are unjust and unreasonable without a complete picture of how they will

interact with the RBA. At the very least, the Commission should defer action on the

proposed revisions until PJM proposes tariff revisions to implement the RBA.



                                                  Respectfully submitted,

                                                  DAVID S. LAPP
                                                  PEOPLE’S COUNSEL
